[{"order":1,"type":"heading","text":"Failover Mechanisms and Connection Pooling (PgBouncer) in PostgreSQL"},{"order":2,"type":"subheading","text":"Introduction"},{"order":3,"type":"paragraph","text":"High availability and resource management are critical components of production-grade PostgreSQL architectures. As connection counts scale, the overhead of maintaining dedicated backend processes per client degrades performance. PgBouncer addresses connection management by pooling client connections, while failover mechanisms ensure continuous availability during primary database node failures."},{"order":4,"type":"subheading","text":"Understanding PgBouncer Pooling Modes"},{"order":5,"type":"paragraph","text":"PgBouncer operates in three distinct pooling modes, each balancing performance and application compatibility differently:"},{"order":6,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Session pooling: The server connection is assigned to the client for the entire duration of the client session. When the client disconnects, the connection returns to the pool. This mode supports all PostgreSQL features."},{"order":7,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Transaction pooling: A server connection is assigned only for the duration of a transaction. Once the transaction completes (COMMIT or ROLLBACK), the connection is returned to the pool. Session-level states (like SET) do not persist across transactions."},{"order":8,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Statement pooling: The most aggressive mode. The server connection is released immediately after each SQL statement execution. Multi-statement transactions are not supported in this mode."},{"order":9,"type":"subheading","text":"Configuring PgBouncer"},{"order":10,"type":"paragraph","text":"The primary configuration file for PgBouncer is pgbouncer.ini. Below is a production-ready configuration utilizing transaction pooling."},{"order":11,"type":"code","text":"[databases]
mydb = host=127.0.0.1 port=5432 dbname=production_db

[pgbouncer]
listen_addr = *
listen_port = 6432
auth_type = md5
auth_file = /etc/pgbouncer/userlist.txt
pool_mode = transaction
max_client_conn = 1000
default_pool_size = 50
min_pool_size = 10
reserve_pool_size = 5
reserve_pool_timeout = 5"},{"order":12,"type":"subheading","text":"Integrating PgBouncer with Failover Mechanisms"},{"order":13,"type":"paragraph","text":"When deploying PostgreSQL with high availability tools like Patroni, repmgr, or Pacemaker, database nodes can change roles (Primary to Standby) during a failover event. Because PgBouncer caches connection strings to specific hosts, handling a failover requires updating PgBouncer configurations dynamically or routing traffic through a Virtual IP (VIP) or DNS load balancer."},{"order":14,"type":"subheading","text":"Using Patroni with PgBouncer"},{"order":15,"type":"paragraph","text":"Patroni can automatically manage PgBouncer configuration and restart it during switchovers or failovers. This is typically configured inside the patroni.yml configuration file under the pgbouncer section."},{"order":16,"type":"code","text":"pgbouncer:
  listen_addr: 0.0.0.0
  listen_port: 6432
  parameters:
    auth_type: md5
    pool_mode: transaction
    max_client_conn: 1000
    default_pool_size: 50
  auth_query: SELECT usename, passwd FROM pg_shadow WHERE usename = $1"},{"order":17,"type":"subheading","text":"Handling Failover via PgBouncer Admin Console"},{"order":18,"type":"paragraph","text":"If you manage PgBouncer manually, you can pause traffic, update the target host in pgbouncer.ini, and reload the service without dropping client connections entirely using the administrative console."},{"order":19,"type":"code","text":"PSQL_PASSWORD=my_admin_password psql -h 127.0.0.1 -p 6432 -U pgbouncer pgbouncer

-- Pause incoming queries to flush active statements
PAUSE mydb;

-- Reload configuration after updating host IP
RELOAD;

-- Resume traffic
RESUME mydb;"},{"order":20,"type":"subheading","text":"Best Practices for Production"},{"order":21,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Always set appropriate timeouts such as query_timeout and idle_transaction_timeout inside PgBouncer to prevent hanging connections."},{"order":22,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Monitor pool exhaustion metrics using Prometheus exporters or direct queries to the SHOW POOLS command."},{"order":23,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Ensure application connection strings point to the PgBouncer port (e.g., 6432) rather than directly to PostgreSQL when transaction pooling is mandated."}]
